newsitem.title: HONG KONG: Renewed U.S. inflation fears seen pressing Asia stocks.
newsitem.headline: Renewed U.S. inflation fears seen pressing Asia stocks.

text.p: Renewed inflation fears in the United States were expected to pressure Asian stocks next week, quashing hopes of rebounds in many centres, brokers said.

"We had expected bargain-hunting in selected blue chips, which have bottomed out, but the Dow's fall will deter the bargain-hunters," said one broker in Jakarta, echoing the sentiment in many other Asian centres.
U.S. blue chips were hammered on Friday after a surprising jump in wholesale prices forced investors to recast their outlook for inflation and interest rates.

The Dow industrials slumped 148 points or about 2.3 percent to close at 6392, its eighth largest decline ever in point terms. The sell-off left the Dow 134 points lower for the week, the fifth week in a row the average showed a loss.

The culprit was a 0.4 percent increase in the U.S. core Producer Price Index (PPI), a measure of inflation at the wholesale level. Analysts said the rise, well above the 0.1 percent economists had expected, increased the odds that the Federal Reserve would raise interest rates again in May. The market's recent woes rank among the worst it has endured since embarking on its stunning ascent in early 1995.

Since its last record close of 7085.16 on March 11, the Dow has shed 693 points, or nearly 9.8 percent, within a whisker of the 10 percent customarily considered to represent a signficiant correction in share prices.
The market's five-week decline marks the first time since late 1991 that it has fallen for such a long period.
Tokyo brokers expected the sharp fall on Wall Street to depress Japanese stocks next week with the key Nikkei average possibly testing its closing low of 17,303 points set on January 10.

On Friday, buy-backs of some financial issues and interest in laggard blue chips boosted the 225-share Nikkei average to close up 361.23 points, or 2.07 percent, at 17,846.98. But that was little changed from the April 4 close of 17,860.59.

"Nikkei futures will probably react to the Dow fall and weaken the Nikkei average enough for it to test the January 10 closing low of 17,303," said Masaaki Higashida, strategist at Nomura Securities Co. Ltd.
Selling in the banking sector would continue, brokers said. "As seen in the previous week, banking sector shares are weak due to dissolution of cross share-holdings," one broker said.

"Such selling is likely to continue but some investors will buy laggard low-priced stocks backed by firm earnings forecasts regardless of how the indices are and regardless of how market sentiment is." Hong Kong stocks are also expected to be pressured by resurgent U.S. interest rate fears, frustrating hopes that the Hang Seng Index might begin a recovery from six-month lows this week.

Hong Kong stocks had finished on a strong note on Friday, with the index rising 157.90 points to 12,516.60 and bringing the week's gains to 312.01 points, or 2.56 percent. Analysts said it had found short-term support around the 12,000 level.
In Taipei, share prices finished sharply lower on Saturday as profit-taking intensified after Wall Street's overnight plunge, but consolidation was forecast for the coming week.
The weighted index ended 105.19 points or 1.22 percent lower at 8,487.89. Turnover was a hectic T$149 billion in the abbreviated Saturday session.

Electronic shares led Saturday's fall, down 2.87 percent, on worries over a probe of certain types of memory chips imported from Korea and Taiwan following a finding by the U.S. International Trade Commission, brokers said.
"The market has risen a lot recently and it is especially sensitive about such bearish news at the moment," one analyst said. "Technically, it opted for a correction as well."

Brokers said investors largely discounted the imminent direct crossings between Taiwan and China after Taiwan approved on Friday four shippers from arch rival China to sail directly across the Taiwan strait, ending a ban dating to 1949.
"The market has expected this to happen. It's not a surprise," an analyst said.
But brokers said shipping shares may have a chance to rise once the direct crossings actually take place.
Brokers were also concerned that the government, and especially the central bank, may issue new warnings about the buoyant market.
In Malaysia, the sharp fall in the Dow was expected to quash any hopes of a rebound on the Kuala Lumpur Stock Exchange.
Stock market analysts said the KLSE Composite Index would open lower on Monday, though the magnitude of the fall may be smaller than in New York.
"The market is already weak due to domestic concerns. The Dow plunge is going to compound the selling," said Liew Yin Sze, regional economist with J.M. Sassoon & Co in Singapore.
He said many overseas funds were already withdrawing from the Malaysian stock market and the Dow fall would accelerate the process.

Analysts said the market continues to digest the impact of the central bank's curbs on property and stock lending. Banks are due to report back to Bank Negara Malaysia by April 15 on how they intend to comply with the new regulations.
"It is possible that the composite index will fall to the 1,100 mark that people were talking about earlier," said an analyst with a Malaysian research firm said.

For the week, the Composite Index of 100 large capitalised stocks closed 1.58 points or 0.14 percent higher from a week ago. On Friday, the index ended down 9.60 points to 1,138.36 points, a decline of 0.84 percent from Thursday.
In the last two weeks, the Composite Index has fallen 79.28 points of 6.5 percent.
An equity analyst with another local research firm said, "I think it will continue to be jittery. There's nothing positive to pick it up in the short-term."
Jakarta stocks were likely to move sideways next week, brokers said.
They said the Dow's fall would further dampen sentiment, which was already weak following recent reports of riots in Central Java.

While expectations of lower values would keep some bargain hunters on the sidelines, brokers said interest in some big-caps such as Telkom and Indofood would likely continue as they were considered to have bottomed out.

On Friday, the Jakarta composite index closed 1.59 points higher at 637.15 against last week's close of 637.43 points. After ending one of its worst weeks with a mini-rally on Friday, Manila stocks are expected to slip back in negative territory on fears of a U.S. rate increase, traders said.
"The 148-point drop on Friday of the Dow Jones will further aggravate negative (local) sentiment," said Noel Reyes, vice president for research at Anscor Hagedorn Securities.
On Friday the main index finished 27.76 points, or 0.94 percent up, at 2,976.78 points in a second straight day of what brokers said was a technically induced rally.
The index suffered a weekly loss of 2.7 percent from 3,060.59 on April 4. Since March 31 when the index was at 3,222.98 and when the downturn began, the index has lost 7.6 percent.
India shares will continue to be rattled by political uncertainty after the defeat of the United Front coalition govenrment in a confidence vote late on Friday.

The ousted United Front has said it will not join rival Congress or the Hindu nationalist Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) in talks to form a new coalition and one senior front official said a snap poll seemed inevitable.
Indian shares closed lower after in special sessions on Saturday but some brokers believed that a widely welcomed budget would still be approved later this month despite the political crisis.
